'NiS Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA corner Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City http: //www.dilg.com.ph OPINION NO. JAN 31 2020 RESIDENTS OF VILLA OLYMPIA SUBDIVISION PHASE 1 Barangay Maharlika, City of San Pedro, Laguna Gentlemen: This has reference to a letter you sent dated 21 November 2019, seeking this Department's legal opinion regarding the road clearing operations involving properties inside private subdivisions. In the letter, in order to ease the traffic situation in the vicinity due to ambulant vendors, the Board of Directors (Board) of the Homeowner's Association (HOA) of Villa Olympus Phase I & IA City of San Pedro, Laguna issued a resolution to open London Street corner Olympia Avenue, a gated street of the subdivision, to establish a livelihood project in a form of a "talipapa" wherein ambulant vendors would conduct their business. However, the HOA Board received a letter from the City Business Permits and Licensing Office requesting for a conference due to a complaint by one Mr. Abulencia, an owner of a commercial building adjacent to the "talipapa", regarding the operations of the "talipapa". After several meetings, the city's presiding officers discovered that the commercial building owned by Mr. Abulencia was constructed without a building permit and that the roof of the building is encroaching along the main sidewalk as well as its sidewalk is elevated. Then in a meeting held on August 15, 2019, in a compromise agreement, it was agreed upon that both illegal structures were to be dismantled. The HOA Board were willing to dismantle the mini market with the condition that the commercial building of Mr. Abulencia will also be dismantled/demolished. Accordingly, the dismantling of the "talipapa" started but the HOA Board noticed that commercial building was not being dismantled. This prompted the HOA Board to write a letter to the City's building official. However, they were informed by the building officials that they can only issue a closure order on every business operating in the commercial building of Mr. Abulencia. Finally, on 15 November 2019, the HOA Board received information that the City's Engineering Department will dismantle/demolish the "talipapa" but not the commercial building. Under this premise arose the request for legal opinion and clarification regarding two (2) issues:

1.) Propriety of the actions of the local government officials in dismantling the "talipapa" despite being in a gated street of a private subdivision; and 2.) Refusal of the local government officials to dismantle/demolish the commercial building of Mr. Abulencia At the outset, this Department would like to clarify that the afore-mentioned letter did not contain the specific reason as to why the "talipapa" was dismantled/demolished by the local government officials. Due to its failure to shed light on whether it was due to the lack of necessary permits or whether it was pursuant to MC No. 2019-1211, enjoining all local officials to exercise their powers essential to reclaim public roads, this Department deems it proper to consider both circumstances in discussing the first issue. Supposing that the dismantling/demolition was due to the failure of the HOA Board to obtain the necessary permits in the construction of the "talipapa", this Department is of the considered view that the city government may properly issue the demolition of the said establishment. Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code, as amended (LGC), authorizes city and municipal governments, acting through their local chief executives, to order the closure and removal of illegally constructed establishments for failing to secure the necessary permits2. The relevant provision of the aforementioned law is quoted hereunder: "SECTION 455. Chief Executive; Powers, Duties and Compensation. — (b) For efficient, effective and economical governance the purpose of which is the general welfare of the city and its inhabitants pursuant to Section 16 of this Code, the city mayor shall: (3) Initiate and maximize the generation of resources and revenues, and apply the same to the implementation of development plans, program objectives and priorities as provided for under Section 18 of this Code, particularly those resources and revenues programmed for agro- industrial development and countryside growth and progress and, relative thereto, shall: (vi) Require owners of illegally constructed houses, buildings or other structures to obtain the necessary permit, subject to such fines and penalties as may be imposed by law or ordinance, or to make necessary changes in the construction of the same when said "presidential Directive During the 4th State of the Nantion Address of the President to Clear Roads of Illegal Structures and Constructions" 2 Section 455(b)(3)(vi), The Local Government Code of the Philippines

construction violates any law or ordinance, or CQ order the demolition or removal of said house, buildinq or structure within the period prescribed by. law or ordinance: [Emphasis and underscoring supplied]. Evidently, mayors are empowered to order the closure and removal of illegally constructed establishments for failure to secure the necessary permits, pursuant to its police power wherein property rights of individuals may be subjected to restraints and burdens in order to fulfil the objectives of the government of promoting the general welfare. Note also that under the LGC, the city and municipal engineer shall also act as the local building officiaP and that under Section 205 of PD 1096 or otherwise known as the National Building Code of the Philippines, except as otherwise provided therein, the Building Official shall be responsible for carrying out the provisions of such Code in the field as well as the enforcement of orders and decisions made pursuant thereto. On the other hand, supposing that the reason for the dismantling the "talipapa" was pursuant with this Department's MC No. 2019-121 this Department would like to qualify. The pertinent provision of Presidential Decree (PD) No. 957, otherwise known as "The Subdivision and Condominium Buyers' Protective Decree", as amended by PD NO. 12164, provides: "Sec. 31. Roads, Alleys, Sidewalks and Open spaces. — Upon their completion as certified to by the Authority, the roads alleys, sidewalks and playgrounds shall be donated by_ the owner or developer to the city or municipality_ and it shall be mandatory for the local governments to accept provided, however, that the parks and playgrounds may be donated to the Homeowners Association of the project with the consent of the city or municipality concerned. No portion of the parks and playgrounds donated thereafter shall be converted to any other purpose or purposes. " [Emphasis and underscoring supplied]. As can be gleaned from the above-quoted provision, the owner as developer of a subdivision is required to provide adequate roads, alleys and sidewalks and donate the same to the city or municipality concerned. It is only after donation that 3 SECTION 477. Qualifications, Powers and Duties. — xxx The appointment of an engineer shall be mandatory for the provincial, city and municipal governments. The city and municipal engineer shall also act as the local building official. 4 Defining "Open Space" in Residential Subdivisions and Amending Section 31 of Presidential Decree No. 957 Requiring Subdivision Owners to Provide Roads, Alleys, Sidewalks and Reserve Open Space for Parks or Recreational Use

these roads, alleys and sidewalks in a subdivision are considered part of the public domain and are within the territorial jurisdiction of the said city or municipality. Hence, before the local government units (LGUs) implement road clearing operations mandated under this Department's MC No. 2019-121 on subdivision roads and sidewalks, there must be a determination whether the roads were already donated by the subdivision owner/developer to the concerned LGU or acquired by the government through expropriation. If the answer is yes, then, the implementing LGU may proceed with the road clearing operations since the subdivision roads and sidewalks are already "public roads". Otherwise, the same must be stopped. We now delve on the second issue regarding the refusal of local government building officials to dismantle/demolish the commercial building of Mr. Abulencia pursuant to this Department's MC No. 2019-121. In this regard, this Department would like to emphasize that the core objective of the memorandum, in compliance with the directive of the President, is the removal of road obstructions through reclaiming roads, and road rehabilitation. Accordingly, the LGUs are enjoined to rid illegal structures which are being used for private ends. Consequently, since the roof of the commercial building of Mr. Abulencia encroaches upon the main sidewalk and its sidewalk is elevated, this Department is of the considered view that such obstructions must be removed pursuant to MC No. 2019-121. Accordingly, if the concerned local government officials refuses to dismantle/demolish the subject commercial building pursuant to MC No. 2019-121 then appropriate administrative cases shall be filed for non-compliance thereof pursuant to Section 60(c) of the LGC and other existing laws and policies. Conversely, as to the commercial building itself, as previously discussed, the mayor has the power to order the closure and the demolition or removal of illegally constructed establishments for failing to secure the necessary permits. We hope to have addressed your concern accordingly. COPY FURNISHED: ELIAS F. FERNANDEZ, JR. CSEE OIC-RegionaI Director DILG IV-A (CALABARZON) 3/F Andenson Bldg. 1, National Highway, Brgy.
